nodeData.note: How a company comes into being in Kenya: what a company is, why it is a separate person from its owners, the types of company, and the steps to register one under the Companies Act 2015.

children.note: A company is a business that the law treats as a 'person' of its own, separate from the people who own and run it. Most serious businesses in Kenya trade as companies.

children.topic: A company is a legal person
children.note: The law lets a company own property, sign contracts, borrow, sue and be sued in its own name, just like a human being can.

manas.q: What does it mean to say a company is a legal person?

children.note: The people who own a company are its members. In a company with shares they are called shareholders.

manas.q: Who are the members of a company?

children.note: Directors are the people chosen to manage the company day to day and make decisions for it. One person can be both a shareholder and a director.
Incorporation is the legal act of bringing a company into being by registering it. Before that, there is no company, only people planning one.

manas.q: What is incorporation?

children.note: In Kenya companies are formed and run under the Companies Act, 2015, which replaced the old Companies Act (Cap 486). It is the law you study in CA21.

Owners' personal property is protected (limited liability), the business can outlive its owners, it is easier to raise money by selling shares, and banks and big customers often prefer to deal with a company.

children.topic: The costs of being a company
children.note: More paperwork and rules: annual returns, keeping registers, audits for many companies, and company tax. Company details are also on a public register.
Once registered, the company is a separate person from its owners. Its debts are its own, and its property is not the owners' property.

Mr Salomon sold his shoe business to a company he controlled and took secured debentures. When it failed, the House of Lords held the company was a separate person, so he was not personally liable and his secured loan was valid.

manas.q: What did Salomon v Salomon & Co Ltd decide?

children.note: It is the starting point for every question on separate personality. Even a company owned and controlled by one person is a different person from that owner.
If a company limited by shares fails, a shareholder only loses what they paid, or still owe, for their shares. Their house, car and savings are safe from company creditors.

manas.q: What is limited liability?

children.note: A company carries on even if its members die, sell their shares or leave. Only a legal process, such as winding up or striking off, ends it.

manas.q: What is perpetual succession?

children.note: Company assets belong to the company, not to the shareholders. A shareholder who takes company money without proper authority can be in trouble, even if they own all the shares.

children.topic: Company can sue and be sued
children.note: Contracts are made in the company's name, so the company, not its owners, sues or is sued on them.
In rare cases courts or statutes ignore separate personality and look at the people behind the company. This is called lifting or piercing the corporate veil.

manas.q: What is lifting the corporate veil?

children.note: Courts lift the veil when a company is a mere front used to dodge an existing legal duty or to cheat, for example a company set up only to escape a promise not to compete.
Insolvency law can make directors personally pay towards company debts if they kept trading to cheat creditors. Check the current Insolvency Act wording.
Usually each company in a group is separate. Only in special cases, such as a clear agency arrangement, will a court treat a subsidiary as acting for its parent.
Courts and tax law may look at who really controls a company, for example to tackle tax avoidance schemes or, historically, to identify enemy control in wartime.
Companies differ by how members' liability is limited and by whether they can offer shares to the public.
Members' liability is limited to any amount unpaid on their shares. This is the usual type for trading businesses in Kenya.

manas.q: What is a company limited by shares?

children.note: Members promise to pay up to a fixed amount if the company is wound up, and usually have no shares. Common for charities, clubs, schools and professional bodies.

manas.q: What is a company limited by guarantee?

children.note: Members have no limit on their liability for company debts if it is wound up. Rare; sometimes chosen for privacy or special professional reasons.

manas.q: What is an unlimited company?

children.note: A company whose articles restrict share transfers, limit the number of members, and stop it inviting the public to buy its shares. Its name ends in 'Limited' or 'Ltd'.

manas.q: What are the key features of a private company?

children.note: A company that may offer its shares to the public and can apply to be listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange. It faces stricter rules, such as a minimum share capital set by law. Its name ends in 'PLC'.

manas.q: What is a public company?

children.note: Every listed company is public, but not every public company is listed. Listing on the NSE adds Capital Markets Authority rules on top of company law.
A company formed outside Kenya that sets up a place of business here must register with the Registrar as a foreign company and name a local representative.
You met partnerships in CA13. A company and a partnership are both ways for people to run a business together, but the law treats them very differently.

children.topic: Separate person vs group of people
children.note: A company is a separate legal person. An ordinary partnership is just the partners themselves trading together.

manas.q: State the main difference between a company and a partnership.

children.note: Shareholders in a limited company risk only their share money. Ordinary partners are personally liable for all firm debts. (An LLP is a middle way.)
Partners usually all manage the business. In a company, shareholders and directors can be different people.
Shares can be sold without ending the company. A partner leaving or dying may end the partnership unless the agreement says otherwise.
A partnership can start with a simple agreement. A company must register, file returns and keep public records, which is more work but builds trust.
A company can sell shares and give lenders security over its assets with a floating charge. Partnerships rely mainly on the partners' own money and loans.
Before a company exists, someone must plan it, find money and do the paperwork. That person is a promoter.
A person who takes steps to form a company and get it going, such as finding premises, investors and directors. Lawyers and accountants acting only in a professional role are not promoters.

manas.q: Who is a promoter?

children.note: A promoter owes duties of good faith to the company being formed. They must not make secret profits and must disclose any personal interest in deals with the company.

manas.q: What duties does a promoter owe?

children.note: A promoter buys land for KES 4,000,000 and sells it to the new company for KES 5,500,000 without telling anyone. The KES 1,500,000 profit can be recovered by the company.
A contract made for a company before it is registered. The company did not exist when it was signed, so under the old common law it could not be bound by it.

manas.q: What is a pre-incorporation contract?

children.note: Promoters bought wine for a hotel company not yet formed. The company was formed but failed, and the promoters were held personally liable because the company could not be party to the contract.

manas.q: What principle comes from Kelner v Baxter?

children.note: The Companies Act 2015 lets a company, once registered, adopt (ratify) a contract made in its name before incorporation. Until then, the person who signed is usually personally liable. Check the Act for exact conditions.
Write the contract so it only takes effect if the company is formed and adopts it, or sign a fresh contract after incorporation.
Companies are registered by the Registrar of Companies at the Business Registration Service (BRS). Applications are made online on the eCitizen platform.
The state body that keeps Kenya's registers of companies, business names, partnerships and charges. The Registrar of Companies works within it.

manas.q: Which body registers companies in Kenya?

children.topic: Step 1: search and reserve a name
children.note: Search the proposed name on the BRS portal and reserve it. A name that is too close to an existing one will be refused.
A private limited company name must end with 'Limited' or 'Ltd'; a public one with 'PLC'. Names that are offensive, misleading, or suggest a link to government need approval or are refused.

manas.q: How must a private limited company's name end?

children.note: Give the company name and type, registered office address, details of directors and shareholders, the share capital and shares taken, and upload IDs and photos.
Under the 2015 Act this is a short statement in which the first members (subscribers) say they wish to form the company and agree to become members.

manas.q: What is the memorandum of association under the Companies Act 2015?

children.note: The company's internal rule book: how directors are appointed, how meetings run, how shares are issued and transferred. It binds the company and its members.

manas.q: What are articles of association?

children.note: Ready-made articles set out in regulations. A company can adopt them in full, change some, or write its own; if it registers none, the model articles apply.

manas.q: What are model articles?

children.note: Members can change the articles by special resolution (a big-majority vote) and must file the change with the Registrar.
Every company must have an official address in Kenya where legal letters and notices can be served. Changes must be notified to the Registrar.
Pay the fees on eCitizen and submit. The Registrar checks the documents and, if all is in order, registers the company. Check current fees on eCitizen.
The Registrar's certificate that the company is formed. It shows the name, registration number and date, and is conclusive proof the company was properly registered.

manas.q: What is the certificate of incorporation?

children.note: A CR12 is an official BRS record listing a company's directors and shareholders. Banks, tenders and buyers often ask for a recent one.
A company must find out and record the real people who ultimately own or control it, keep this register, and lodge it with the Registrar. This fights money laundering and hidden ownership.

manas.q: What is a beneficial owner?

children.note: Register for a company KRA PIN and the right taxes, open a bank account, set up statutory registers, appoint a company secretary if required, and file annual returns.
A company can change its type after it is formed by re-registering. This needs a members' resolution, changed articles and a filing with the Registrar.
Done when a business wants to raise money from the public. It must meet the public company rules, such as minimum share capital, and change its name to end in 'PLC'.

manas.q: Why might a private company re-register as public?

children.note: A public company that no longer needs public money can go private to cut costs and red tape. Members who object may be able to apply to court.
Changing to unlimited needs every member's agreement, because each takes on unlimited liability. An unlimited company can also become limited.
A sole trader or partnership trading under a registered business name can form a new company and move the business into it. This is a new registration, not a re-registration.
Scenarios showing the rules at work for small Kenyan businesses. All names and figures are made up for practice.
Wanjiru runs 'Afya Bora Chemist' in Nairobi as a sole trader. She wants to protect her home and bring in an investor.
A private company limited by shares fits: limited liability, room for a few shareholders, and no need to sell shares to the public.
She reserves 'Afya Bora Pharmacy Limited', adopts the model articles, and lists herself and her investor as directors and shareholders.
After paying and getting the certificate, she records the beneficial owners, gets a company KRA PIN and opens a company bank account.
She sells the stock and equipment to the company under a written agreement and updates the pharmacy's licences into the company's name.
Afya Bora Pharmacy Ltd fails owing a supplier KES 2,000,000. Wanjiru holds 50,000 shares of KES 20 each, KES 1,000,000 in total, with KES 700,000 paid.
The debt is the company's (Salomon). Wanjiru can only be made to pay the unpaid KES 300,000 (1,000,000 − 700,000). Her house is safe unless the veil is lifted.
Before registration, Otieno signs a KES 600,000 shop-fit contract 'for Matatu Spares Ltd'. The company is never registered.
There is no company to bind, so Otieno is personally liable for the KES 600,000. Had the company been registered, it could have adopted the contract.

children.topic: Choosing a type for a school club
children.note: A parents' group wants a body to run a school sports club with no profit for members.
A company limited by guarantee: no shares, members' liability limited to a small promised sum, and profits go back into the club.
Small mix-ups that cost marks in company formation questions.
In a limited company the company pays its own debts. Owners lose only unpaid share money, unless the veil is lifted.
Lifting the veil is an exception, not the rule. Always start with Salomon, then explain the special reason a court might ignore it.
The memorandum is a short statement by the first members. The articles are the detailed internal rules.
Public means it may offer shares to the public. Listed means its shares trade on the NSE. A public company need not be listed.
Cap 486 was replaced by the Companies Act 2015. Use the 2015 Act and current BRS practice in your answers.
Short exam-style questions. Try each one before opening the answer steps.
Explain the principle with a case and give two consequences.
A registered company is a legal person separate from its members: Salomon v Salomon & Co Ltd.
Limited liability for members, and perpetual succession. You could also mention owning property and suing in its own name.

children.topic: Q2: Four situations for lifting the veil
children.note: Give four situations where the courts or statute may ignore separate personality.
Fraud or sham company; fraudulent or reckless trading by directors; agency in a group of companies; tax avoidance or enemy control cases.
Kamau signed a supply contract for a company before it was registered. Advise him.
A company cannot be bound by a contract made before it existed; the signer is usually personally liable (Kelner v Baxter).
Once registered, the company can adopt the contract under the 2015 Act, which shifts liability. Next time, make the contract conditional on incorporation.

nodeData.note: How a company raises money from owners (shares) and lenders (debentures), and the rules that protect that money for creditors. Builds on topic 1, Forming a company, under Kenya's Companies Act 2015.

children.topic: What share capital is and why
children.note: Share capital is the money owners put into a company in return for shares. It is the company's base fund, and the law protects it so lenders and suppliers can trust the company.

children.topic: A share = a piece of ownership
children.note: A share is one unit of ownership in a company. It gives the holder rights, such as a vote and a dividend, set by the articles and the terms of issue.
People who hold shares are the company's members. Their liability is limited to any amount still unpaid on their shares.

manas.q: What is the limit of a shareholder's liability in a company limited by shares?

children.note: Creditors cannot chase shareholders' personal property. So the law keeps capital inside the company as a cushion for paying debts.
Equity (shares) makes you an owner who shares profits and risk. Loan capital (debentures) makes you a lender who gets interest and must be repaid.
Accountants and lawyers use several words for share capital. Each one measures a different stage, from shares created to cash actually received.
The fixed face value of each share stated when it is issued, for example KES 10 a share. It is not the market price.

manas.q: What is the nominal (par) value of a share?

children.note: The most share capital a company could issue, once stated in its memorandum. Older Kenyan companies still show it; check the current rules and the articles for any cap.
The nominal value of shares actually given out to members.

manas.q: What is issued share capital?

children.note: The part of the nominal value of issued shares that the company has asked members to pay so far.

manas.q: What is called-up share capital?

children.note: The part of called-up capital that members have actually paid. Any shortfall is 'calls in arrears' and members still owe it.

manas.q: What is paid-up share capital?

children.note: Nominal value not yet called. It is money members still promise to pay if asked, for example in a winding up.
A company may have more than one class of share. Each class has its own rights, set out in the articles or terms of issue.
The main owners' shares. They usually carry votes and get whatever profit is left after others are paid, so their risk and reward are highest.

manas.q: What rights do ordinary shares usually carry?

children.note: Shares that come first for a fixed dividend, and often for return of capital on winding up. They usually have limited or no votes.

manas.q: What are preference shares?

children.note: Cumulative: a missed preference dividend carries forward and must be paid before ordinary dividends. Non-cumulative: a missed one is lost. Preference shares are presumed cumulative unless the terms say otherwise.

manas.q: What is a cumulative preference share?

children.note: Shares issued on terms that the company will buy them back later. They must be fully paid before redemption.
Preference shares that get their fixed dividend and also share in extra profits with ordinary shareholders.

Class rights are the special rights of one class, like a fixed dividend. They can be changed only with that class's consent, usually by a set majority vote or written consent, as the articles and the Act require.

manas.q: How can class rights be varied?

children.note: Holders who did not agree can usually apply to the court within a short time to cancel the change if it is unfairly harmful to them. Check the current time limit in the Act.
Directors give out (allot) new shares under rules that protect existing members from having their stake watered down.
Allotment is the company deciding who gets new shares. Directors need power to allot, from the articles or a members' resolution.

manas.q: What is allotment of shares?

children.note: After allotting shares the company must file a return of allotment with the Registrar of Companies within the deadline in the Act.
When new ordinary shares are issued for cash, existing members must first be offered them in proportion to what they hold. This stops their share being diluted.

manas.q: What are pre-emption rights?

children.note: Private companies may exclude it in their articles, and members can disapply it by special resolution in set cases. It does not apply to shares issued for non-cash assets or bonus shares.
Shares cannot be issued for less than their nominal value. A KES 10 share must bring in at least KES 10.
Shares sold above nominal value. The extra over nominal goes to a share premium account, not to share capital.

manas.q: What is a share premium?

children.note: Share premium is treated like capital. It can pay up bonus shares and write off the costs of the issue that created it, but it cannot pay dividends.

manas.q: Name two allowed uses of the share premium account.

children.note: Shares can be paid for with land or a business instead of cash. For public companies, such assets usually need an independent valuation first.
Two common ways to issue more shares to existing members. One brings in cash; the other brings in none.
New shares offered to existing members for cash, in proportion to their holding, usually below market price. Example: 1 new share for every 5 held.

manas.q: What is a rights issue?

children.note: A member who does not want to buy can often sell their right to someone else, or let it lapse.
Free shares given to members by turning reserves into share capital. No cash comes in; reserves fall and share capital rises.

manas.q: What is a bonus issue?

children.topic: Which reserves pay for bonus shares
children.note: Share premium, capital redemption reserve or retained profits can be used. Using capital reserves first keeps profits free for dividends.
After a bonus issue the member holds more shares but the same percentage of the company. The share price usually falls in proportion.
The capital maintenance rule says money paid in as capital should stay in the company and not be handed back to members except under strict rules.

manas.q: What is the capital maintenance rule?

children.note: Dividends may be paid only out of profits available for the purpose: accumulated realised profits less accumulated realised losses. Never out of capital.

manas.q: What are distributable profits?

children.note: A public company must also keep its net assets at least equal to called-up capital plus undistributable reserves after the dividend.
A member who knew or should have known a dividend was unlawful must repay it. Directors who approved it may be personally liable.
A company may reduce share capital, for example to wipe out past losses or return extra cash, but only with members' and creditor safeguards.
Any company: special resolution confirmed by the court. A private company may instead use a special resolution backed by a directors' solvency statement. Check the Act for details.
Creditors may object in the court route. In the solvency route, directors who make a false statement face penalties.
A company may buy its own shares or redeem redeemable shares if the articles allow and the Act's conditions are met. Payment normally comes from distributable profits or a fresh issue.

manas.q: Where must the money for a share buy-back normally come from?

children.note: When shares are bought back out of profits, an amount equal to their nominal value is moved from profits into a capital redemption reserve, so total capital is kept.

manas.q: What is a capital redemption reserve?

children.note: A public company generally may not help someone buy its own shares, such as by lending them the money. There are exceptions; private companies have more freedom. Check the Act.
Companies also borrow. A debenture is the document showing a company's debt, often secured by a charge over its assets.
A written promise by a company to repay a loan with interest. Debenture holders are creditors, not members.

manas.q: What is a debenture?

children.note: Shareholders own and get dividends only from profits. Debenture holders lend, get interest whether or not there is profit, and are repaid before members on winding up.

manas.q: Give three differences between shares and debentures.

children.note: Security over a specific asset, like a building or vehicle. The company cannot sell it without the lender's consent.

manas.q: What is a fixed charge?

children.note: Security over a changing group of assets, like stock and debtors. The company deals with them freely until the charge crystallises.

manas.q: What is a floating charge?

children.note: The floating charge becomes fixed on the assets held at that moment, for example on winding up or receivership, or a default event in the deed.
On insolvency, fixed charge holders are paid from their asset first. Floating charge holders come after preferential creditors.
Most charges must be registered with the Registrar within the deadline in the Act. An unregistered charge is void against a liquidator and other creditors, though the debt itself remains.

manas.q: What happens if a registrable charge is not registered in time?

children.note: Practice entries for a Kenyan company. All figures are made up; check that debits equal credits each time.
Mavuno Ltd issues 100,000 ordinary shares of KES 20 nominal at KES 50 each, all paid in cash.
Dr Bank 5,000,000 / Cr Share capital 2,000,000 / Cr Share premium 3,000,000. Debits 5,000,000 = credits 5,000,000.
Jua Kali Ltd has 400,000 shares of KES 10 and share premium of KES 600,000. It makes a 1-for-4 bonus issue.
400,000 ÷ 4 = 100,000 new shares × KES 10 = KES 1,000,000 to capitalise. Use all KES 600,000 premium, and KES 400,000 from retained earnings.
Dr Share premium 600,000 / Dr Retained earnings 400,000 / Cr Share capital 1,000,000. Debits 1,000,000 = credits 1,000,000. No cash moves.
Pwani Pharmacy Ltd has 500,000 shares of KES 10. It offers 1 new share for every 5 held at KES 25, and all are taken up.
Dr Bank 2,500,000 / Cr Share capital 1,000,000 / Cr Share premium 1,500,000. Debits 2,500,000 = credits 2,500,000.
Tumaini Ltd issues 200,000 shares of KES 10. It calls KES 6 a share; holders of 190,000 shares pay.
Matatu Movers Ltd issues 10% debentures of KES 3,000,000 at par for cash.
On issue: Dr Bank 3,000,000 / Cr 10% Debentures 3,000,000. Yearly interest 3,000,000 × 10% = 300,000: Dr Interest expense 300,000 / Cr Bank 300,000.
Kilima Ltd buys back 50,000 of its KES 10 shares at nominal value, paying from distributable profits.
Dr Share capital 500,000 / Cr Bank 500,000. Then Dr Retained earnings 500,000 / Cr Capital redemption reserve 500,000. Each entry balances.
Mix-ups that cost marks in Company Law and accounts questions.
Share capital is always nominal value only. Anything above nominal goes to share premium.
Share premium is capital, not profit. It cannot fund a cash dividend.

children.topic: Thinking a bonus issue brings cash
children.note: A bonus issue only moves reserves into share capital. A rights issue brings cash.
Called-up is what was asked for; paid-up is what was received. The gap is calls in arrears.
Debenture holders are creditors. They are paid interest, not dividends, and usually have no vote.
Late or missing registration makes the security void against a liquidator, leaving the lender unsecured.
Short exam-style questions. Try each before opening the answer.
Distinguish a fixed charge from a floating charge (4 marks).
Fixed: specific asset, no dealing without consent, ranks first. Floating: shifting class of assets, free dealing until crystallisation, ranks after preferential creditors.
A company with 300,000 KES 10 shares makes a 1-for-3 rights issue at KES 18, fully taken up. Give the journal.
New shares 100,000. Dr Bank 1,800,000 / Cr Share capital 1,000,000 / Cr Share premium 800,000. Debits 1,800,000 = credits 1,800,000.

children.topic: Q3: Can this dividend be paid?
children.note: A private company has realised profits of KES 4,500,000 and realised losses of KES 1,200,000 and 800,000. Directors want a KES 3,000,000 dividend.
Distributable = 4,500,000 − 1,200,000 − 800,000 = KES 2,500,000. A KES 3,000,000 dividend is too high; at most KES 2,500,000 may be paid.
